People were supported to understand their rights, including their human rights, rights under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and their rights under the Equality Act 2010.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: We looked for evidence that there was an inclusive and positive culture of continuous learning and improvement that was based on meeting the needs of people who used services and wider communities. We checked that leaders proactively supported staff and collaborated with partners to deliver care that was safe, integrated, person-centred and sustainable, and to reduce inequalities. At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant there were widespread improvements in service leadership. Leaders and the culture they created assured the delivery of high-quality care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Leaders had the experience, capacity, capability and integrity to ensure that the organisational vision could be delivered and risks were well managed.

Leaders at every level were visible and lead by example, modelling inclusive behaviours. Staff felt leaders were inclusive and capable. They felt leaders were approachable and they could raise any concerns with them. ‘Cuppa with the CEO’ allowed staff to openly talk to the CEO in a neutral environment, invitation was advertised on the weekly bulletin and staff from both hospitals had this opportunity.

High-quality leadership was sustained through safe, effective and inclusive recruitment and succession planning. Leaders went through a robust selection, assessment and interview process and recruitment checks before getting appointed into roles, ensuring they met the personal specification criteria to perform the role effectively. We saw the fit and proper person policy was in date and next due for review in March 2027.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: There was a culture of speaking up where staff actively raised concerns and those who did (including external whistleblowers) were supported, without fear of detriment. When concerns were raised, leaders investigated sensitively and confidentially, and lessons were shared and acted on. Staff felt confident to raise concerns. The trust had a freedom to speak up guardian with whom staff could raise concerns about any issues.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There were clear and effective governance, management and accountability arrangements. Staff understood their role and responsibilities. Managers could account for the actions, behaviours and performance of staff. Staff were clear about their roles and responsibilities, and they could access relevant information about patients’ care and treatment.

The systems to manage current and future performance and risks to the quality of the service took a proportionate approach to managing risk that allowed new and innovative ideas to be tested within the service. The service had a clear governance structure with defined roles and responsibilities. The trust had business continuity plans in place for various scenarios. They had systems to back up data and return to paper in the event of a system failure. Information was shared with staff through;

  • Blogs
  • Monthly Newsletters
  • Weekly bulletin
  • Monthly learnings from death

Weekly bulletins were inclusive and kept staff up to date with what was happening in the trust, social events, updates on training and policies.

There were robust arrangements for the availability, integrity and confidentiality of data, records and data management systems. Information was used effectively to monitor and improve the quality of care. A certificate was awarded for completing a data security and protection toolkit self-assessment to demonstrate the department was practicing good data security and personal information was handled correctly from 2023 to 2024. The confidentiality and data protection policy and the information security policy were in date and next due for review in May 2027 and July 2025 respectively.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders ensured that people using the service, their families and carers were involved in developing and evaluating improvement and innovation initiatives. Staff informed us the service was intended as a 111, however, they publicised the unit's phone number in 2021post COVID. This increased the number of people who had access to the service and were able to take advantage of the services offered.

Staff and leaders had a good understanding of how to make improvements happen. The approach was consistent and included measuring outcomes and impact. We saw evidence of examples of adhering to external recommendations. Two out of the 4 examples had been implemented and closed. A log was kept for National Patient Safety Alerts. Three alerts were opened and were due action. 12 had been actioned and closed and two were not applicable to the trust but justifications had been provided for this.

There were processes to ensure that learning happened when things go wrong, and from examples of good practice. Leaders encouraged reflection and collective problem-solving. Patient group directions (PGDs) completion had improved since our last inspection where 50% were out of date. The majority of PGDs reviewed were in date and in line with national guidelines.

Staff were supported to prioritise time to develop their skills around improvement and innovation. There was a clear strategy for how to develop these capabilities and staff were consistently encouraged to contribute to improvement initiatives. All staff were eligible to participate in the Trust’s in house CPD accredited Improvement Contributor training. This 12-hour course teaches staff the principles of lean continuous improvement and how to apply them to their work areas to improve services by removing or reducing waste in processes. They are then equipped with the knowledge and skills to work on a small-scale improvement project which delivers tangible measurable change using the Plan-Do-Study-Act approach.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders are open and transparent, and they collaborated with all relevant external stakeholders and agencies. The service set up a tissue viability winter collaboration with a nearby trust. Whereby said nearby trust funded 1.0 Whole Time Equivalent in THHT tissue viability team. Supporting high pressure wards.

The service was included in all relevant discussions surrounding urgent and emergency care delivery for the Hillingdon Borough. An example discussion with partners was how Mount Vernon site could support the winter pressures of 2022 driven by the Strep A outbreak. The site was not utilised but the discussion surrounded placing a GP from the community at the site in a similar manner that had been undertaken during the pandemic. A further example of community relations was adjusting the process for patients obtaining an appointment, developing from 111 only to patients calling the service directly to describe symptoms and obtain an appointment if necessary or suitable.

Staff and leaders worked in partnership with key organisations to support care provision, service development and joined-up care. Staff informed us they had good working relationships with other services. They liaised with GP practices, acute hospitals and other community teams to care for patients. GP interface virtual meetings were set up to discuss communications with GP and understand imaging requests and reports.

Staff and leaders engaged with people, communities and partners to share learning with each other that resulted in continuous improvements to the service. They use these networks to identify new or innovative ideas that can lead to better outcomes for people. Staff provided assessment and treatments for children at home, staff provided and assisted with respiratory assessments, set up intravenously antibiotics, asthma stretch and weaning plans, gastroenteritis management, phototherapy, temperature management and fluid challenge.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Leaders ensured there was a shared vision and strategy and that staff in all areas knew, understood and supported the vision, values and strategic goals and how their role helped in achieving them. The vision was ''to deliver the best possible care for all who need our services''. With a focus on quality, people, performance, finance, partnerships and strategic programmes.

  • Goals
  • Have a rating of good across all services and for well-led.
  • Deliver the 4 pillars of their people strategy, and have staff recommending the trust as a place to work.
  • Deliver right care at the right time for patients.
  • Live with means, and support financially sustainable system.
  • Help lead care within the Hillingdon system.
  • Lead delivery of a series of high profile complex programmed which support the organisations long term plans.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Leaders took action to continually review and improve the culture of the organisation in the context of Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI). EDI was a priority for the trust in 2024 - 2025. The Inclusion lead and inclusion team could be contacted by staff. Staff could get involved in Trust’s EDI agenda by:  

  • Being an EDI champion: support the EDI lead and drive the Trust’s strategy.  
  • Taking part in the reciprocal mentoring scheme: and make an impact to someone else’s life.  
  • Being an interview panel expert: and ensure fairness in selection process  
  • Joining staff EDI networks  
  • Supporting and joining social events 
  • Sharing personal stories and reasons you are #proudto 
  •  Staff had access to multiple networks including: 
  • Multicultural Network  
  • Able 4 All (Disability Network)  
  • LGBT+ Allies Staff Network  
  • Women’s network  
  • International Nurses’ Network 

Leaders took active steps to ensure staff and leaders were representative of the population of people using the service. The trust workforce was made up 59.1% BME, 38.8% White and 2.2% Unknown/Not Disclosed. The data from ESR showed that there was an under-representation of Black Asian and Minority Ethnics (BAME) staff in clinical posts at Band 3, 4 and 7 and above, and under-representation of BAME staff in non-clinical posts at Band 3,4,5,6,7 and above.

The relative likelihood of White applicants being appointed from shortlisting compared to BAME applicants slightly decreased from x1.39 to x1.34. There were 14 disciplinary cases opened during the rolling 24-month period; 6 were against BAME staff and 8 against White staff. This was a reduction on last year. The likelihood of BAME staff entering a formal disciplinary process, compared to White staff, increased to 0.86%. 59.6% BAME staff accessed non mandatory training, compared to 37.9% white staff. The relative likelihood of White staff accessing non-mandatory training and CPD compared to BME staff was 0.97%. BAME representation on the Executive Board decreased this year. Non-Executive BME Board membership remained static for a third year.
